blocks.text: An adult cuts his hand on a rusty spade and has not had a tetanus vaccine for fifteen years. He is given a booster dose. Within days his antibody level against tetanus toxoid is far higher than it was after his first-ever dose as a child. That difference is immunological memory, and it is the reason booster vaccines work.

blocks.markdown: The **humoral response** is the production of antibody by B cells. Most protein antigens trigger a **T-dependent** response, which needs help from CD4⁺ T cells and produces class-switched, high-affinity antibody and memory. Polysaccharides can sometimes activate B cells without T cell help (T-independent responses), producing mainly IgM with little memory, which is why conjugate vaccines link polysaccharide to a protein carrier.

**T-dependent B cell activation, step by step.**

1. A naive B cell in a lymph node follicle binds antigen through its B cell receptor (BCR), internalises it and presents peptide on **MHC class II**.
2. The B cell moves to the border of the follicle and T-cell zone, where it meets an activated CD4⁺ T cell of matching specificity (a **T follicular helper cell**, Tfh). The T cell receptor recognises the peptide-MHC II complex.
3. Co-stimulation follows: **CD40 ligand (CD154)** on the T cell binds **CD40** on the B cell, and cytokines (e.g. IL-21, IL-4) are secreted.
4. Some activated B cells form short-lived **plasmablasts** secreting early IgM; others enter the follicle and found a **germinal centre**.

blocks.title: Germinal centre
blocks.text: A structure within a lymph node follicle where activated B cells proliferate, undergo somatic hypermutation and class switching, and are selected for higher-affinity receptors. It produces long-lived plasma cells and memory B cells.

blocks.markdown: **Inside the germinal centre.** The **dark zone** contains rapidly dividing centroblasts, where activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) causes somatic hypermutation of the variable genes. Cells then move to the **light zone** as centrocytes. There **follicular dendritic cells** display antigen and Tfh cells provide survival signals. B cells whose mutated receptors bind antigen better compete successfully and survive; the rest undergo apoptosis (**affinity maturation**). Class switching (IgM to IgG, IgA or IgE) is also directed by Tfh cytokines. Selected cells leave as **long-lived plasma cells** (which home to bone marrow and secrete antibody for years) or **memory B cells**.

blocks.title: Where is the defect?
blocks.prompt: A boy with a mutation in the gene for CD40 ligand makes IgM in response to a protein antigen but little IgG, IgA or IgE and no germinal centres. Using the steps above, explain why.

steps.text: The B cell can still bind antigen and present peptide, and the Tfh cell can recognise it, so initial IgM production (including extrafollicular plasmablast IgM) is preserved.
CD40L on the T cell cannot signal through CD40 on the B cell, so the co-stimulation needed for germinal centre formation is absent.
Without a germinal centre there is no AID-driven class switching or affinity maturation, and little memory.
Therefore IgM is the dominant antibody, and IgG, IgA and IgE are very low.

blocks.answer: Defective CD40L-CD40 signalling blocks germinal-centre events, leaving IgM without switching or memory.

blocks.markdown: **Kinetics.** After a first encounter with antigen (the **primary response**), there is a **lag phase** of several days before antibody is detectable, as naive B cells have to find antigen and T help. IgM appears first, followed by IgG; the response peaks after about 1 to 2 weeks and then declines. On a second encounter (the **secondary response**), memory B and T cells respond: the lag is shorter (often 1 to 3 days), the rise is faster, the peak titre is higher (frequently ten-fold or more), the antibody is mainly **IgG** with higher **affinity**, and it persists longer.

blocks.caption: A four-fold or greater rise between paired sera is conventionally taken as evidence of recent exposure or vaccination

blocks.markdown: **Passive immunity from the mother.** Of all antibody classes only **IgG** crosses the placenta, by active transport through the **neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)** on syncytiotrophoblast cells. Transfer is greatest in the third trimester, so a preterm infant has less maternal IgG. The newborn is thus protected against the pathogens the mother has been exposed to or vaccinated against, without having to make its own antibody. This **passive immunity** decays with the half-life of IgG (about three weeks), so maternal IgG falls over the first months of life, while the infant's own production gradually rises. Breast milk (especially colostrum) adds secretory IgA that protects the gut surface locally.

blocks.title: How much maternal IgG remains?
blocks.prompt: A newborn has a serum IgG specific for a pathogen of 32 units/mL, all maternal. Assume a half-life of 21 days and no new production. How much remains at 63 days?

steps.text: Work out the number of half-lives.
Interpret: only one-eighth of the maternal antibody remains by nine weeks, illustrating why protection is temporary and why infant vaccination schedules begin in the first months.

blocks.title: Memory is the reason boosters work
blocks.text: Memory B cells (from the germinal centre) are numerous, have high-affinity, class-switched receptors and are readily activated, so a second dose gives a faster and larger response than the first.

points: T-dependent B cell activation requires antigen presentation on MHC class II, Tfh help (CD40L-CD40, cytokines) and germinal-centre events: somatic hypermutation, class switching and selection.
Secondary responses have a shorter lag, higher titre, more IgG and higher affinity than the primary response.
Maternal IgG crosses the placenta through FcRn, protecting the newborn passively until it wanes.

questions.stem: Which interaction provides the key co-stimulatory signal from a T follicular helper cell to a B cell?

options.text: CD28 on the B cell binding CD80
CD40 ligand on the T cell binding CD40 on the B cell

questions.correctOptionText: CD40 ligand on the T cell binding CD40 on the B cell

distractorRationale.a: CD28/CD80 is the T cell co-stimulation by APCs, not the B cell help signal.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: CD40L-CD40 engagement is essential for germinal centre formation.
distractorRationale.c: CD8 and MHC I relate to CTLs.

questions.explanation: CD40L on activated helper T cells engages CD40 on B cells, delivering signals needed for proliferation, class switching and germinal-centre reaction. Cytokines such as IL-21 and IL-4 add further direction.

questions.stem: In which germinal-centre compartment does somatic hypermutation chiefly occur?

options.text: Light zone, in follicular dendritic cells

distractorRationale.a: Light zone is where selection occurs.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: centroblasts divide rapidly and mutate their V genes.

questions.explanation: Centroblasts in the dark zone divide quickly and undergo AID-mediated mutation of the variable genes; centrocytes then move to the light zone, where affinity is tested by antigen on follicular dendritic cells and Tfh help.

questions.stem: A patient previously immunised against hepatitis B receives a booster dose. Compared with the primary response, which is expected?

options.text: Shorter lag, higher titre, predominantly IgG with higher affinity
No antibody because memory cells are inactive

questions.correctOptionText: Shorter lag, higher titre, predominantly IgG with higher affinity

distractorRationale.b: Correct: memory cells give faster, higher, IgG-dominated responses.
distractorRationale.c: Memory cells are primed to respond.
distractorRationale.d: IgE is not the main response to vaccines.

questions.explanation: The secondary response is faster and larger and has more class-switched, higher-affinity IgG than the primary response because memory B cells are present.

questions.stem: Which cells are responsible for the rapid secondary response?

distractorRationale.a: Naive cells drive the slower primary response.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: memory B cells respond quickly.
distractorRationale.d: Mast cells are not responsible for antibody memory.

questions.explanation: Memory B cells generated during the primary response are long-lived and have high-affinity, class-switched receptors, so they respond rapidly on re-exposure.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin class is actively transported across the placenta?

distractorRationale.a: IgM is too large and is not transported.
distractorRationale.d: IgE does not cross to a significant extent.

questions.explanation: Only IgG is actively transported across the placenta, using FcRn on the syncytiotrophoblast, providing passive immunity to the fetus and newborn.

questions.stem: A neonate has 80 units/mL of maternal IgG specific for a pathogen. Assume a half-life of 21 days and no new antibody production. What is the concentration after 84 days (in units/mL)?
questions.explanation: 84 days is 4 half-lives (84/21 = 4). The concentration is 80 × (1/2)^4 = 80/16 = 5 units/mL. This is why the passive protection of maternal IgG is temporary.

questions.stem: Paired sera from a patient show a vaccine-specific antibody titre of 1:16 before and 1:512 after a booster dose. Calculate the fold rise in titre.
questions.explanation: Fold rise = 512/16 = 32, well above the four-fold rise taken as significant. This reflects a vigorous secondary response from memory B cells.

questions.stem: Outline the steps of T-dependent B cell activation, from antigen binding to the production of plasma cells.
markingGuide: B cell BCR binds antigen, internalises and presents peptide on MHC class II
Germinal centre: proliferation, somatic hypermutation (dark zone), selection (light zone), class switching
Differentiation to plasma cells and memory B cells
questions.explanation: The B cell needs antigen presentation and T cell help; the germinal centre then refines the response.

questions.stem: Contrast primary and secondary antibody responses in lag time, magnitude, isotype and affinity, and explain the cellular basis of the difference.
markingGuide: Primary: longer lag, lower peak, IgM then IgG, lower affinity
Secondary: shorter lag, higher peak, IgG dominant, higher affinity
Memory B cells with class-switched, affinity-matured receptors
Memory cells have lower activation threshold and are more numerous than naive specific cells
questions.explanation: The secondary response is driven by memory B cells generated in germinal centres during the primary response.

questions.stem: Explain how a newborn obtains protection against infection from maternal antibody, and why the protection is limited in time.
markingGuide: IgG is actively transported across the placenta via FcRn
Greatest transfer in the third trimester
Newborn has maternal antibody without making its own (passive immunity)
IgG half-life about three weeks, so levels decline over months
Breast milk IgA adds local gut protection
questions.explanation: Maternal IgG provides immediate, short-lived protection that wanes as it is catabolised.
